item.description: ［ニューヨーク １４日 ロイター］ - ニューヨーク外為市場では、ドルがユーロなどの主要通貨に対し上昇した。米国の９月の...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ＮＹ外為市場＝ドル上昇、9月ＣＰＩ上振れで追加利上げ観測再燃 5:42 配信

２０１１年１月撮影　REUTERS/Kacper Pempel

［ニューヨーク　１４日　ロイター］ - ニューヨーク外為市場では、ドルがユーロなどの主要通貨に対し上昇した。米国の９月の消費者物価指数（ＣＰＩ）の伸びが加速したことを受け、連邦準備理事会（ＦＲＢ）が今月末に開く会合で追加利上げを決定するとの観測が再燃したことでドルに買いが入り、主要通貨に対するドル指数は約１年半ぶりの高値を付けた。ただ、その後はＦＲＢは慎重な姿勢を維持するとの見方が再び広がり、ドルは上げ幅を縮小した。

労働省が朝方発表した９月のＣＰＩは前年比３．７％上昇と、伸びは８月の３．４％から加速。エコノミスト予想の３．６％も上回った。変動の大きい食品とエネルギーを除くコアＣＰＩは前年比２．６％上昇。８月の２．４％から加速し、予想の２．５％も上回った。

ＦＲＢの金融政策を巡っては、ニューヨーク連銀のウィリアムズ総裁やボウマンＦＲＢ副議長らからハト派的な発言が相次いでいたが、こうした発言による影響は９月ＣＰＩ統計を受けて後退した格好となった。また、インフレ圧力が経済全体に広がりつつあるとの懸念が広がる中、ＦＲＢがこの日の午後に発表した地区連銀経済報告（ベージュブック）で、米国の労働市場は雇用も解雇も低水準にとどまる状態が続く一方、一部地域でインフレ圧力が強まっていることが示された。

ステート・ストリート（ボストン）のシニア・グローバル市場ストラテジスト、マービン・ロー氏は「ドルを買い進める新たな材料が加わった」と指摘。メシロー・カレンシー・マネジメントのシニア投資ストラテジスト、ウト・シノハラ氏は「労働市場の弱さを示す兆候が出ていることで、物価安定と最大雇用というＦＲＢが担う２つの責務は互いに緊張関係にある」と指摘。「個人消費、労働市場、物価圧力を巡る状況は、１５日に発表される小売売上高、新規失業保険申請件数、卸売物価指数（ＰＰＩ）などの指標でより明確になる」と述べた。

ＦＲＢは９月１５─１６日の連邦公開市場委員会（ＦＯＭＣ）で０．２５％ポイントの利上げを決定。利上げは２０２３年７月以来、３年２カ月ぶりで、決定は全会一致だった。９月のＣＰＩ統計発表直後、今月２７─２８日のＦＯＭＣで追加利上げが決定される確率は約４５％と、ＣＰＩ統計発表前の約２２％から上昇した。ただその後は利上げ観測はやや後退し、ＣＭＥフェドウォッチによると、１０月のＦＯＭＣで金利据え置きが決定される確率は６５％。同時に、２０２７年末までに合計約７９ベーシスポイント（ｂｐ）の利上げが実施されるとの予想も織り込まれている。

アンジェレス・インベストメンツのマイケル・ローゼン最高投資責任者（ＣＩＯ）は、投資家の間で米国がインフレ抑制に取り組む姿勢への信認が低下しつつあると指摘。「金利上昇に支えられ、ドル高が進んでいる」とし、「ＦＲＢが大幅な利上げによって景気後退を招くか、米政府の通商政策や移民政策が修正されない限り、インフレは低下しない」と述べた。

終盤の取引で主要６通貨に対するドル指数＜=USD＞は０．３４％高の１０２．５３。朝方の取引では１０２．９４まで上昇し、２０２５年４月以来の高水準を付けていた。

ユーロ／ドル は０．４１％安の１．１１５２ドル。一時約１７カ月ぶりの安値を更新した。英ポンド／ドルは０．５９％安の１．３１７７ドル。

ドルは対円では０．０８％安の１５８．１６円と、小幅ながら下落した。

ドル／円　ＮＹ終値 158.31/158.34

始値 158.43

高値 158.94

安値 158.06

ユーロ／ドル　ＮＹ終値 1.1156/1.1159

始値 1.1189

高値 1.1198

安値 1.1114

Netflix to cut about 1,000 jobs amid slower growth

Netflix plans to cut around 1,000 jobs amid slowing revenue growth and reports of declining viewing time on its streaming platform.

NEW YORK: Netflix will cut about 1,000 jobs, or 6 per cent of its workforce, US media reported on Wednesday (Oct 14), as the streaming platform experiences slower growth. When contacted by AFP, the company did not immediately respond. "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources," co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in an internal memo, according to several US media outlets. Now firmly established at the top of the video streaming market, Netflix is no longer able to grow at the same pace as before.

In the second quarter, revenue rose 13.4 per cent from the same period a year ago, slower than the 16.2 per cent rate in the first quarter. The Los Gatos, California-based company is forecasting 11.7 per cent growth in the just-finished third quarter. Several media outlets reported a decline in time spent on the platform after years of uninterrupted growth.

Related:

Paramount settles with US states to clear Warner Bros mega-merger

In early July, Bloomberg reported that average viewership for a series drops after the first season. "Netflix's layoffs show that even the top streaming companies are not immune to stagnation and financial difficulties," commented Emarketer analyst Ross Benes. "While the company will expand its sports roles, it's cutting back at a time when revenue matters much more than subscriber additions," he said. "With pressure mounting, Netflix will look to turn the tide by getting a boost from low-cost content." The company's stock has fallen 15 per cent since the start of the year.

item.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
item.description: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk's SpaceX had restricted military-grade Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk's [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"SpaceX had restricted "military-grade" Starlink services"], hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses. The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." WHAT IS STARLINK? Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX (SPCX.O) , is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers. Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions. WHAT IS STARSHIELD? Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone. Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads. The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024. Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since [USN:L1N31S38K TEXT:"Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022"]. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque. Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the [USN:L6N41W1B2 TEXT:"Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services"] used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal. [USN:L6N4290XG TEXT:"Britain has also adopted Starshield"]. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters. Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

item.title: Pope Leo back on his feet after shock cancer diagnosis
item.description: Pope Leo's recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room, the Vatican said.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:

World

Pope Leo back on his feet after shock cancer diagnosis

Pope Leo's recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room, the Vatican said.

Pope Leo arrives at Gemelli Hospital ahead of the pontiff's surgery to remove a lung nodule in Rome, Italy, on Oct 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Guglielmo Mangiapane)

15 Oct 2026 02:42AM (Updated: 15 Oct 2026 07:24AM)

FAST

VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo 's recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room and eating normally, the Vatican said on Wednesday (Oct 14), after doctors announced the 71-year-old pontiff was being treated for lung cancer . World leaders, Catholics across the globe and senior cardinals at the Vatican have offered prayers for Pope Leo after he had part of his right lung removed in an operation on Tuesday. Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on Wednesday showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy. The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

Pope Leo normally follows a very busy schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17 and the Vatican press office said on Wednesday that "nothing has changed" regarding the planned trip. However, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said on Wednesday that the dates could change because of the amount of time his recovery would take. The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world 's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.

PRAYERS FOR POPE LEO A prayer was recited for Pope Leo to have a good convalescence and complete healing during an open-air Mass in St Peter's Square on Wednesday following the surgery. The pope has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer , and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during Tuesday's operation in an effort to eliminate all cancer ous tissue. Human lung s have five lobes - three in the right lung and two in the left. The operation lasted about 90 minutes and was completed without complications, the pope 's lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr Luigi Carbone, said late on Tuesday. The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. Dr Serena Ricciardi, a lung cancer specialist at Rome's San Camillo Forlanini Hospital, said that if the cancer had not spread to Pope Leo 's lymph nodes, the surgery may have been sufficient for treatment. "If there are no further issues or lymph node involvement, we could consider the surgery curative," she told Reuters. "The disease has been completely removed." Pope Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.

Related:

What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis

Pope Leo recovering after lung cancer operation

ENGAGEMENTS CANCELLED UNTIL NEXT WEEK The Vatican said this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and that all his public engagements had been cancelled until Oct 20. The Mass on Wednesday was the closing act of an assembly of bishops called by Pope Leo to discuss the Church's family life teachings, the largest gathering of Church leaders so far during this papacy. Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle led the service in place of Pope Leo . The pope last week approved Tagle as the dean of the Church's College of Cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role. Political leaders offered messages of support. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the pope , an American who was born in Chicago. "May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," he said on X. Rubio met Pope Leo at the Vatican in May. There was no immediate response on social media from US President Donald Trump, who has criticised the pope , or from Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.title: Even ASML's strong earnings can't save it! U.S. chip stocks' slump intensifies, with industry index at risk of losing a trillion dollars in market value
item.description: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 4% intraday on Wednesday, heading for a six-day losing streak, which would mark its longest losing streak in nearly 17 months. Over the past six days, more than half of the index’s components have fallen at least 10%. ASML is positioned upstream in the semiconductor industry chain. Although strong demand for its lithography equipment indicates that chip manufacturers are still planning capacity expansion, it does not directly prove that the downstream customers of these chip makers will continue to purchase chips at the same pace. While the AI-driven rally has yet to be disproved, the market is raising the threshold for returns.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: The chip stock sell-off, which had just eased during Tuesday's session, intensified again on Wednesday. Memory chip stocks such as Micron Technology and SK hynix weakened once more, and the industry benchmark Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) once fell by over 4% intraday, set to mark its sixth consecutive day of losses. Media outlets report that with concerns mounting over rising interest rates, high valuations, and the costly buildout of AI infrastructure, the total market capitalization of SOX components faces the risk of evaporating by more than $1 trillion. As of Wednesday, June 14 (U.S. Eastern time), when SOX fell over 3% intraday, the index had accumulated a six-day decline of 10%, with over half of its constituents dropping at least 10% over the period. This correction is evolving from short-term profit-taking into a comprehensive test of the AI investment thesis. September’s U.S. CPI inflation was stronger than expected, reinforcing market anxiety about further Fed hikes. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan earlier warned the AI industry could face funding constraints. Even strong results and upgraded sales guidance from semiconductor equipment leader ASML failed to effectively lift chip stocks. The real question now is not merely whether AI demand remains robust, but whether massive capital expenditures can translate into sustainable earnings growth, and whether current valuations have already priced in future profits. SOX Faces Six-Day Losing Streak, Global Chip Stocks Risk Nearly $1 Trillion in Lost Market Value During Wednesday's session, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index hit fresh intraday lows with a drop close to 4.2%, on track to close down for the sixth straight session—marking the longest losing streak since May 2025. At the individual stock level, the correction has spread from memory chips to chip design and manufacturing equipment. According to Bloomberg, over half of SOX constituents have dropped at least 10% in the last six trading days. Arm's U.S. shares (ARM) have fallen nearly 20% over the same period, Applied Materials (AMAT) about 15%, Intel (INTC) approximately 11%. GlobalFoundries (GFS) is the only constituent to post a gain during this timeframe. On Wednesday, Arm plunged over 6% intraday, Intel over 4.6%. Memory stocks, after a brief respite on Tuesday, weakened collectively again: SK hynix's U.S. shares (SKHY) fell over 5.8%, SanDisk (SNDK) dropped 4.9%, Micron Technology (MU) lost 3.5%, and both Western Digital (WDC) and Seagate Technology (STX) slumped over 3% intraday. From Korea and Japan to the U.S., memory chip stocks have already seen severe corrections, and now the decline is spreading further into chip design and equipment manufacturers, showing that investors are reducing exposure across the semiconductor sector. Bloomberg notes that, based on recent declines, SOX constituents are at risk of losing over $1 trillion in market value. This does not mean all that value has already vanished, but rather that if the sell-off continues, the global semiconductor industry may face a dramatic valuation retracement. Rising Inflation, Rate Hike Fears Rekindled, AI High Valuations Under Pressure One major factor fueling the continued chip stock decline is a tightening macro interest rate environment. U.S. September inflation data beat market expectations, with consumer price increases at their highest since April, largely driven by higher fuel costs. This reinforced expectations that the Fed may keep hiking rates, and even if the Fed holds steady later this month, investor perceptions about the future rate path have shifted. For high-valuation tech stocks whose earnings outlook depends on future growth, rising rates mean lower discounted future cash flows and higher costs for financing and expansion. Semiconductor firms, benefiting from AI infrastructure buildout but facing heavy capital expenditure and lengthy payback periods, are especially sensitive to rate changes. Meanwhile, the AI trade itself is under renewed scrutiny. Earlier this week, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likened some AI fever investors to casino gamblers and warned the industry could face funding constraints—further fueling concerns about the sustainability of the AI investment boom. In recent years, investors have been willing to pay premiums for rapid computing power demand growth; now, the market is taking a harder look at companies’ financing abilities, capex size, and the speed at which profits actually materialize. When inflation pushes up rate expectations, capital costs rise, and valuation pressures mount, even strong long-term demand can’t prevent severe stock price corrections. ASML’s Strong Results—Why Can’t They Save Chip Stocks? This week, as chip stocks fell further, semiconductor equipment titan ASML reported robust quarterly results and raised its full-year sales guidance, with strong multi-year equipment demand from customers. Yet, the earnings report failed to reverse the broader chip stock downturn. Barron's analysis points out that a key reason is that ASML sits upstream in the semiconductor supply chain. Strong demand for its lithography equipment shows that chipmakers are still planning to expand capacity, but doesn't directly prove that downstream chip buyers will keep purchasing at the same pace. ASML’s customers include chipmakers like TSMC and Intel, while the real drivers of the current AI investment cycle are end customers such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and other hyperscale data center operators. For chipmakers, equipment orders and long-term capacity planning matter, but more direct impacts on revenue and profits come from whether downstream buyers keep ordering chips—and whether those purchases yield enough returns. ASML's strong performance demonstrates ongoing resilience in AI-related equipment demand, but that alone doesn't dispel market worries about capex efficiency in AI. In other words, order visibility for equipment makers and profit realization for chipmakers are not the same thing. Furthermore, strong demand for ASML’s equipment could have another effect: if tight supply pushes up ASML’s product prices, customers like TSMC and Intel may face higher equipment procurement costs in the future. For companies already facing massive investments to build advanced process capacity, this could further heighten capex pressure. Therefore, ASML’s results failing to lift the whole chip sector doesn’t necessarily mean AI demand is weakening, but rather reflects a market now wanting to see proof that the entire value chain can sustainably profit from AI investment—not just upstream order growth. Wall Street Cuts Outlook: AI Investment to Shift from Spending to Profits Ulrich Hofmann-Burchardi, from UBS Chief Investment Office, noted in a Wednesday research report that pressure on global chip stocks continues to mount. She believes intensifying AI competition, growing funding needs, and rising interest rates could amplify volatility at times, but this correction is more a market expectations reset than a collapse of the AI investment case. This judgment highlights a current market divide: on one hand, AI infrastructure buildout could last for years; on the other, investors are doubting whether this surge in capital spending is sustainable and whether the resulting profits will meet previously lofty projections. Bloomberg points to an upcoming important test: Anthropic’s investor event, reportedly held in San Francisco on Wednesday. Wall Street hopes the AI company will reveal revenue run rates, to better assess if AI company income growth can sustain ever-expanding computing investment. UBS recommends investors focus on whether AI spending can deliver sustainable profit growth, and whether AI applications on the enterprise and consumer sides keep widening. Compared to simply tracking capex totals, these metrics better help determine if today’s investment fever yields stable commercial returns. If AI firms can keep growing revenue and profitability—and prove that huge infrastructure outlays deliver reasonable returns—then the present correction is more likely a recalibration of valuations and expectations. Conversely, if spending outpaces revenue and cash flow improvement, market tolerance for high valuations could fall further. AI Boom Not Disproved, but the Market Is Raising Return Thresholds From SOX’s losing streak, to ASML’s stout earnings failing to spark a rebound, to inflation and rate expectations weighing afresh, today’s chip stock landscape signals investors are shifting from chasing AI-driven growth to scrutinizing real economic returns from AI investment. This doesn’t mean AI demand has collapsed. ASML's orders and sales guidance still show strong semiconductor equipment resilience. Yet, for chip manufacturers and AI infrastructure firms, the market wants more solid proof that ever-increasing capex will translate into matching income, profits, and cash flow. In this context, over $1 trillion in potential market cap at risk reflects not only the scale of recent sell-offs, but also a change in market pricing logic: AI may remain a powerful long-term growth driver, but companies can no longer rely solely on a growth story to fetch premium valuations. Going forward, key variables for chip stocks stabilizing will include AI companies’ revenue run rates, return on capital spending, and their financing capacity in a higher-rate environment.

US inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike this month back on table

US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent in September, driven by higher gasoline prices, increasing pressure on households and complicating the Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates.

A motorist fills up his tank at a gas station amid a fuel shortage in Denpasar, Bali, Indonesia, Wednesday, Oct 14, 2026. (Photo: AP/Firdia Lisnawati)

FAST

WASHINGTON: US consumer prices accele rate d in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labour Department on Wednesday (Oct 14) showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. Financial markets now see the Fed eral Reserve's interest rate decision this month as a closer call than before the data was released. The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump's approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78 per cent of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages. "The inflation we're experiencing right now is largely the result of erratic policy from the executive branch," said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the Century Foundation, a progressive think tank.

"Worse still, the directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains. This administration has also been wholly unwilling to moderate the pace of the AI and data-centre buildout." The CPI rose 0.6 per cent last month after climbing 0.4 per cent in Aug us t, the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics said. The increase in the CPI was in line with economists' expectations.  In the 12 month s through September , the CPI advanced 3.7 per cent after rising 3.4 per cent in Aug us t. A 9.1 per cent surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month . The US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Other motor fuels, which include diesel, soared 11.9 per cent last month and were up 60.9 per cent on a year-over-year basis. Diesel prices at the pump are at record highs, and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket. Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1 per cent in both July and Aug us t. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1 per cent over the month , but rose 1.8 per cent on a year-over-year basis. Beef prices dropped 1.0 per cent in September and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9 per cent. But prices for non-alcoholic beverages surged 0.9 per cent, while fruits and vege table s cost 0.5 per cent more.

CORE INFLATION ABOVE EXPECTATIONS Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3 per cent in September , matching the gain in Aug us t. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would rise 0.2 per cent. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4 per cent increase in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners' equivalent rent rose 0.3 per cent. There were increases in the costs of recreation and education. Prices for us ed cars and trucks increased 0.7 per cent, while airline fares rose 1.2 per cent amid higher jet fuel prices. Apparel prices climbed 0.3 per cent. In the 12 month s through September , core CPI inflation increased 2.6 per cent after advancing 2.4 per cent in Aug us t. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2 per cent inflation target. The core CPI measure is lagging core PCE inflation , which increased 3.0 per cent in Aug us t, beca us e of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets. Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed 's Oct 27 to 28 policy meeting to roughly 52 per cent from about 22 per cent prior to the CPI report, CME Gro up 's Fed Watch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and Aug us t.

Related:

New White House spokeswoman heavy on Trump praise, light on questions in debut

Dollar gains, Wall Street stocks fall after hot inflation data

US Treasury yields were mostly higher while the dollar advanced vers us a basket of currencies. US stocks opened lower. The Fed in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the month s ahead. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rate s in December. The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase next year. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6 per cent cost-of-living adj us tment for Social Security and S up plemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programmes benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.content:encoded:
米中間選挙・トランプ大統領がアラスカ州で遊説…物価高で崖っぷち　それでもMAGA派が“トランプ推し”の理由【news23】

TBSテレビ

2026年10月15日(木) 01:52

国際 news23

逆風でも支える岩盤支持層“MAGA派”がトランプ氏を推す理由

牙城で吹き荒れる逆風は、トランプ氏自身の失速のあらわれでもあります。

政権発足から1年10か月。ロイター通信の世論調査では、支持率が過去最低水準の32％に。一方で、この約3割の人たちが、何があってもトランプ氏から離れない「岩盤支持層」とされています。

「MAGA派」と呼ばれる熱狂的な支持者たちは、いまのトランプ氏に何を期待しているのか。

ペンシルベニア州に住むクズマさんは、自他ともに認めるMAGA派です。

トランプ支持者“MAGA派”　クズマさん

「誰もがMAGAであるべきだ。みんなアメリカが偉大であってほしいと思っている」

争点となっている「物価高」の批判は、メディアによる誇張だと主張します。

トランプ支持者“MAGA派”　クズマさん

「昔から言うように、嘘を繰り返せば人々は信じ込むんだ」

そんなクズマさんの心配ごとは、中間選挙の「投票率」。トランプ氏に直接投票することはできないため、支持者の関心がどこまで高まるかが焦点と言われています。

世論調査では、前回の大統領選挙でトランプ氏を支持した人のうち、中間選挙での投票に約半数が「熱心」と答えた一方、約2割は「関心がない」と答えています。

トランプ支持者“MAGA派”　クズマさん

「トランプのための選挙だと理解しなければ困ったことになる。もし中間選挙に敗れれば、我々はトランプ大統領を失ってしまう」

“崖っぷち”の中間選挙で、MAGAのトランプ支持者たちはどう動くのでしょうか。

item.title: Ukrainian drones hit Russia's top data centre in attack on AI ambitions
item.description: The attack follows a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres.

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's top data centre in attack on AI ambitions

The attack follows a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres.

A man walks outside an office building housing a branch of Russia's largest bank Sberbank in Moscow, Russia, Dec 5, 2025. (Photo: REUTERS/Ramil Sitdikov)

15 Oct 2026 12:43AM

MOSCOW: Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre on Wednesday (Oct 14), part of a series of attack s appearing to target Moscow's ambitions to develop Russian artificial intelligence capabilities on a par with those from the US and China. The strike on the Balakovo data centre , owned by Sberbank, the country's largest bank and technology company, followed three attack s in the past week on data centre s owned by Russian technology group Yandex. "We confirm that the data processing centre was attack ed. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption," Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters. Russian President Vladimir Putin held a previously unannounced meeting on Wednesday with top officials on "information security", in which Sberbank CEO German Gref took part. The Kremlin s ai d that the meeting was not linked to the attack s on data centre s. Russia's state RIA Novosti news agency reported in 2024 that the Sberbank centre hit on Wednesday would host Russia's biggest supercomputer, which is scheduled to go into operation in 2027.

The Yandex data centre s, hit earlier, hosted all three of that company's operating supercomputers. Neither Yandex nor Sberbank has s ai d whether supercomputers, used to tr ai n the AI models, were damaged in the Ukrainian attack s. Along with Yandex, its m ai n domestic rival, Sberbank is Russia's leading developer of artificial intelligence. The domestic market is shared between Sberbank's GigaChat model and YandexGPT.

DIFFICULTIES PURCHASING CHIPS Both companies have invested heavily in the development of their models but lag global leaders in the United States and China by up to nine months, according to Sberbank's own estimates, partly due to Western sanctions which hinder Russia's access to the most advanced hardware. "It's clear what difficulties we face when purchasing modern graphics processing units. Both we and Yandex suffer from this," Gref s ai d on Sep 29, calling it the biggest reason why Russia lags behind the US and China in AI . Sberbank is in talks to buy chips from Chinese makers, but in an interview with Reuters on Jun 3, Vedyakhin s ai d that US chipmaker Nvidia's NVDA.O monopoly on its CUDA software platform, which has become an AI industry standard, is an even greater problem. Yandex s ai d previously that its supercomputers operated on Nvidia A100 chips, a model launched in 2020 and since then succeeded by more advanced H100 chips. Sberbank has two functioning supercomputers. The most advanced one, called Christofari Neo, ranked 167th in the Top 500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers, is located in Moscow and is based on Nvidia A100 chips. Yandex's most advanced Chervonenkis supercomputer is ranked 101st in the same list. IT expert Mikh ai l Klimarev told Reuters it could take a long time to replace the chips due to Western sanctions, while damage to the supercomputers could set back the Russian AI industry, which already suffered from sanctions. "The equipment is being imported, but it's done at a high cost, through indirect routes. First, you need to negotiate so that someone is willing to sell it to you and is not afr ai d of sanctions," he s ai d.

PROTECT ASSETS Some commentators compared the lack of reported disruption at state-controlled Sberbank with Yandex - whose taxi and food delivery units had reported disruptions - saying it showed that Sberbank's centre s are better protected. "This is a great example of what a business owner can do to protect their assets," wrote military blogger Alexander Kots. Under an August decree by Putin, the state can take over administration of poorly protected facilities. The Sberbank site is located close to the Balakovo nuclear power plant, which the data centre uses as an energy source, and the Saratov hydroelectric power plant. No damage was reported to either plant from the attack . Ukr ai ne says it is responding to Russian attack s on its own data sites. Both countries have attack ed each other's refineries, power stations, ports and e-commerce companies. Russia's digital development ministry s ai d this week it was in talks with the military on protecting the data centre s, while some lawmakers called for them to be moved underground where the hardware will be out of reach for drones . "We need a so-called Doomsday data vault," Valery Yermakov, deputy CEO of state-controlled Rostelecom, another major data centre operator, told a conference in Moscow.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.title: Copper price forecasts lifted for 2026 but tariff “collapse” still on the table
item.description: Macquarie’s collapse scenario needs Washington to rule tariffs out, which it rates least likely. More likely is limbo past January 1, with 1.5 million tonnes of US copper staying exactly where it is.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price forecasts lifted for 2026 but tariff “collapse” still on the table

Staff Writer | October 14, 2026 | 9:31 am Critical Minerals   Markets   China   Latin America   USA   Copper

Where do we send these? Credit: Glencore

Copper pulled back from a three-week high on Wednesday after US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table, and word of a preliminary deal to avert a strike at BHP’s Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, took some of the supply premium out of the price.

Comex copper for December delivery traded at $6.6695 a pound (about $14,704 a tonne) late morning in New York, down 0.8%, after touching $6.7890 earlier in the session. The most-active contract’s record settlement of $6.89 was set on September 9 , the day before a report that the White House tariff plan had stalled knocked more than 5% off the price.

In London, three-month copper climbed as far as $14,700 a tonne, its highest since September 23, before easing to $14,532 by early afternoon. Cash copper settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and $14,741 on Tuesday, and LME inventories have fallen for seven straight sessions to 229,650 tonnes.

US consumer prices accelerated in September on a surge in gasoline costs, and the CME’s FedWatch tool put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s late-October meeting at about 44%, double the day before, Reuters reported. New York Fed President John Williams said he still sees one more hike this year.

Two sources told Reuters that Escondida’s supervisors’ union and the company had reached a preliminary agreement , which members were voting on Wednesday morning, and a union leader told Bloomberg a deal was “virtually done”. Unions at Antofagasta’s Centinela returned to talks on Tuesday after a week-long stoppage, while the open pit at Codelco’s El Teniente remains shut after a deadly landslide .

Click on chart for live prices.

Copper’s 2026 advance has forecasters raising their numbers for the second time in three months, and with the metal averaging $13,471 a tonne for the year to date, the 2026 revisions mostly bring the sheet into line with the tape.

Macquarie now has copper averaging $13,573 this year, BMO Capital Markets $13,619 and BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, $13,500, up from the $12,700 it moved to in July . The differences open up from next year, and they come down to how much of the 1.5 to 2 million tonnes of copper now sitting in the United States is counted as surplus.

“The great copper gamble”

Macquarie, which in July called the rally “running ahead of reality” , has lifted its 2027 average by 14% to $12,750 and pushed the cycle low to $12,000 in the fourth quarter of next year from $11,000 a quarter earlier, while its long-term price rises to $10,500 a tonne in 2025 dollars.

Prices “have disconnected from the fundamentals and could arguably move higher or lower depending on the outcome of the Section 232,” the bank’s strategists write in a quarterly compendium whose copper chapter is headed “The great copper gamble”, listing the metal among its preferred commodities for the next six to nine months “but very binary”.

The fundamentals as Macquarie counts them are a 223,000-tonne surplus this year after a 531,000-tonne disruption allowance, and surpluses averaging more than 700,000 tonnes a year from 2027 as mine supply grows 4.9% next year and 4.3% in 2028, with Collahuasi, Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula and Centinela ramping up, Tia Maria starting and Cobre Panama back in full from mid-2027.

Global demand growth slows to 1.5% in 2027 on its numbers, with none at all in China, where construction-related copper use is shrinking 9% a year and air conditioner makers are “again looking at aluminium substitution.”

Visible stocks worldwide are up 300,000 tonnes this year, but that is the US build; everywhere else they are down 168,000 tonnes, and Macquarie says sentiment will not turn until LME and Shanghai inventories start rising again, either quickly on a tariff decision or gradually as its forecast surpluses feed through.

Macquarie’s four tariff scenarios run from a January 1 that passes with no announcement at all, which it rates most likely, to a definitive decision against a duty, which it rates least likely: “the CME price will most likely collapse, taking the LME price with it, and the arb will invert,” with surplus US stocks reappearing in LME warehouses in the US and Asia.

A tariff announced six to eight weeks ahead of implementation would pull a last wave of metal into the US and leave the rest of the world “very tight”, while a formal six-month delay would see the spread fade as it did for platinum and palladium after the critical minerals decision.

Expectations are also growing that a scrap export ban will be folded into any decision; an immediate ban would take about 600,000 tonnes a year of contained copper off the world market.

“Has the market misread US inventory?”

BMO Capital Markets arrives at a very different place from a similar starting point. Its quarterly price deck, published two days before Macquarie’s, raises its long-term copper price by 47% to $16,000 a tonne in real terms, or $18,000 nominal by 2030, with $14,675 for 2027 and $16,000 for 2028, and the bank puts itself 46% above consensus on the long-term number. Its market balance is close to balanced throughout: an 83,000-tonne surplus this year, then small deficits from 2027.

The argument turns on what the US hoard, now close to 2 million tonnes on BMO’s estimate, or about a year of American consumption, actually represents. China’s refined copper imports have run below trend and its exports above trend since the tariff trade began, a cumulative swing of about 1.6 million tonnes on a net basis, which BMO reads as Beijing allowing its strategic reserve to run down while Washington built one.

“Instead of there being a build in above ground inventory over the last 2 years, there has been a geographical redistribution from ‘not visible’ to ‘visible’, meaning today’s price of ~$14,500-15,000/t is fundamentally supported,” the bank writes. Had China bid for metal alongside the US, “copper prices today would in fact be much, much higher,” and at some point China will want to restock.

BMO expects no tariff decision before the US midterms in November, which may see copper “pause for breath” and keep the Comex-LME spread narrow, but says investors it talks to are coming around to the view that the US stockpile “could simply stay in situ for many more years.”

Rising dependence on scrap, with China’s secondary refined output heading for 3.3 million tonnes this year from 2.8 million, is the other leg of its case: scrap is the marginal unit, and it only comes out at higher prices.

BMI sits between the two. It still views the rally “as having extended beyond what fundamentals alone would suggest” and has the market in a 43,000-tonne surplus this year, but has cut its 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.1% from 2.4% with Chilean output down 4%, and expects a deficit from 2027 that widens to 1.7 million tonnes by 2035 as demand grows 3% to 4% a year on grids, EVs and data centres.

Its 2027 forecast is $12,900, rising to $15,000 in 2029 and an unchanged $17,000 in 2035. The International Copper Study Group, meeting this week, lifted its 2026 surplus to 104,000 tonnes and kept 2027 at 368,000 tonnes.

The arb has gone, the metal has not

The spread that built the US stockpile has all but disappeared on a spot basis. Comex October copper at $6.62 a pound trades below LME cash, which at Tuesday’s $14,741 works out to $6.69, and John Gross of The Copper Journal calculates the month-to-date average has flipped to an 85-point LME premium from a 17-cent Comex premium in June.

Most of that is London’s doing: the backwardation that put cash $164.50 over three months at Monday’s settlement, since narrowed to $115.50, reflects how little spot metal is left outside the US.

Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has offered customers a record premium of $347 a tonne for 2027 supply, 10% above this year’s level, Benchmark Minerals reported, and a company spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a lot of material has relocated to the US, leaving warehouses quite empty.”

Further down the curve the premium survives. December Comex at $14,704 a tonne sits about $170 over LME three-month, which Macquarie read at the end of September as the market pricing a 10% chance of a 15% duty (on Wednesday’s prices the same arithmetic gives about 8%).

That is too little to pull fresh shipments across the Atlantic, but enough to keep what is already there in place as long as the Comex curve pays traders to hold it. The tonnes still arriving are cargo booked months ago: Comex stocks rose another 6,500 tonnes last week to 713,000 tonnes, with 100,000 tonnes of African and South American copper due through October.

Deutsche Bank takes the stockpiling argument furthest. Daniel Ghali, the bank’s new head of metals research, told the Wall Street Journal that with China adding to its strategic reserve for decades and the tariff threat pulling metal into American sheds, the two countries could be sitting on 71% of the world’s supply by the end of the year. On that trajectory copper “simply won’t be available” to users elsewhere by the end of 2028, an outcome averted only by prices high enough to force substitution into aluminium.

He sees $10 a pound, or $22,050 a tonne, in the second quarter of 2027, almost 50% above current levels. Even a decision against tariffs may not free the metal, he told the paper, since the LME has warehouses in the US and copper may simply be shuffled between American sites rather than leave the country.

Gross points to copper’s premium over aluminium, which hit a record $5.08 a pound in September, more than double its July 2022 low. “Clearly, this rising premium cannot continue indefinitely, but who among us will step forward to say it’s at the top?” he writes. His September monthly report makes the longer point: China consumed 58.9% of the world’s refined copper last year, up from 12.4% in 2000. “There are too many copper eggs in China’s basket.”

Miners still pricing $5 copper

Copper producers fell with the metal on Wednesday, Lundin Mining down 3.9%, Freeport-McMoRan 3.7%, Southern Copper 3.3% and Teck Resources 2.9%, but the year has been kind. Southern Copper is up 44.1% in 2026, taking its market value to $169 billion, with Glencore ahead 38.6%, BHP 38.0% and Freeport 37.4% at a $100 billion valuation. Teck has gained 36.1% and Anglo American 29.2%. Lundin has managed 13.0%, Antofagasta 7.5% with Centinela on strike, and First Quantum 3.0%.

RBC Capital Markets calculates that North American copper producers at 1.0 times net asset value imply a copper price of $5.03 a pound, from $5.98 for Freeport down to $3.96 for Ivanhoe Mines, against a futures price near $6.70. The group trades at 0.9 times net asset value, in line with its 10-year average.

Comex copper is up more than 18% in 2026.

item.title: B.C. home sales fall 9% in September amid interest rate speculation
item.description: Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province’s real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: VANCOUVER — Home sales in British Columbia dipped again in September, with the province’s real estate board saying interest rate hike speculation weighed on the market. The British Columbia Real Estate Association says in a release that just over 5, 250 homes were sold last month, down about 9 per cent from the same month in 2025. Home sales were about 26 per cent lower than the 10-year average for B.C. for the month of September. The association says sales volume for residential transactions in B.C. last month was $4.9 billion, down 11 per cent from a year ago, while the average price on the Multiple Listing Service fell 2.4 per cent to just over $924,000. Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson says in a statement that the declines come after “an encouraging summer” where B.C. showed signs of recovery, but spiking oil prices have prompted speculation on whether the Bank of Canada will raise interest rates. About 51,000 homes have been sold in B.C. so far in 2026, down about 6 per cent from the same period last year, with sales in September falling year-over-year in every region other than South Peace River and the Kootenays. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

Safety of Indian seafarers, tankers raised in Doval’s conversation with Iranian counterpart, says MEA

PTI

14 October, 2026 09:47 pm IST

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) The issue of safety and security of Indian seafarers and tankers figured in the recent phone conversation between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday.

The two sides also discussed regional situation and international developments, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in response to a query during his bi-weekly media briefing.

The telephonic conversation that took place on October 12 focused on the prevailing security situation in West Asia.

Show Full Article

Jaiswal was asked the details about the outcome of the conversation, and if India raised the issue of attacks on Indian-flagged vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Regarding the conversation that our National Security Advisor had with his counterpart in Iran, this conversation happened on October 12. National Security Advisor spoke to the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, His Excellency Dr Mohsen Rezaei,” he said.

“They discussed bilateral issues. They also discussed regional situation and international developments. And during the meeting, the safety and security of Indian seafarers was raised, as the safety and security of Indian tankers was also raised,” Jaiswal added.

New Delhi has maintained that the repeated attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf are “completely unacceptable and must cease immediately”.

India on Wednesday condemned the string of attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, saying the “totally unacceptable” acts need to cease immediately.

New Delhi also asserted that it remains committed to doing the best for the welfare and well-being of Indian nationals abroad.

India has been consistently calling for resolution of the West Asia crisis through dialogue and diplomacy.

New Delhi has also been concerned over spate of attacks on merchant ships in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz.

When asked about the proposed India-US bilateral trade agreement, Jaiswal said External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has spoken about it at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. Both sides remain engaged on this particular matter for a mutually beneficial bilateral trade agreement, he said.

India and the US are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a “landing point”, Jaishankar said on Tuesday, while noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.

Asked if the H-1B issue and the recent comments made by the US vice president will be raised during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s upcoming visit to India, Jaiswal just said “several issues of bilateral nature will be discussed”.

Rubio will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the US Department of State said on Tuesday.

Jaiswal was also asked about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s expected visit to Canada, and whether the bilateral trade deal is likely to be concluded before the visit.

On the trade deal, Jaiswal said the fifth round of negotiations happened in Ottawa a week ago or so, and both sides remain committed to a mutually beneficial Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).

PM Modi, after a telephonic conversation with his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney on Tuesday, said he had a “warm and productive” conversation with him and both leaders agreed to build on the “positive momentum” in bilateral ties.

Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, who is on a working visit to India, on Wednesday met Modi. The PM said they had a productive discussion on further strengthening India-Canada ties in trade, technology and energy.

Asked about the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council raising issues related to recent communal incidents, Jaiswal said, “It is our expectation that such issues will be addressed by the Bangladeshi side.”

On the Home Ministers’ Meeting of BIMSTEC here on Tuesday, the MEA spokesperson said, “We had participation from all BIMSTEC countries, and post the conversation, the meeting, a Delhi Declaration was also adopted, wherein the commitment of all the BIMSTEC countries to strengthen cooperation across a range of areas including fight against terrorism, counter-narcotics measures, and anti-money laundering cooperation.”

“It is our expectation that with this inaugural dialogue, there will be a stronger security cooperation among all members,” he said.

On the recent comment made by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Geneva over the recent detention of thousands of protesters in Delhi, he reiterated that it was “unwarranted” and at the same time “unacceptable because it amounts to interference” in India’s internal affairs.

They have, it seems, an approach of “extreme selectivity” and if they continue on this path, then obviously, it will lead to loss of faith in multilateralism, Jaiswal said, adding that at the same time, it “undermines their credibility as an organisation”. PTI KND KVK

item.title: Statistics Canada reports building permits up $1.1B in August at $13.6B
item.description: Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector. The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August. The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion. The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August. The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion. The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

Airtel’s Mittal says his firm ahead of Musk’s Starlink in India’s Satellite internet queue

PTI

14 October, 2026 08:49 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal on Wednesday said his satellite communications venture Eutelsat OneWeb was significantly ahead of Elon Musk’s Starlink in the queue to launch services in India, adding a fresh twist to a public dispute over regulatory approvals and competition in the country’s satellite internet market.

Meanwhile, government sources, responding to the controversy surrounding Starlink and Musk’s recent claims, said any company operating in India must comply with the law of the land and added that the Centre’s position has been clear and consistent throughout.

“Government’s position has been very clear, and was so even at the time they had applied, that if you don’t follow Indian laws, you cannot do business here…So to do business here you have to follow Indian laws,” sources said.

Show Full Article

At the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Mittal said his satcom venture Eutelsat OneWeb is significantly ahead of Elon Musk’s Starlink in the satcom queue in India, having applied five years ago, and added that he would be happy to receive the go-ahead at least a few days before the US tech billionaire.

“I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back,” Mittal said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026. “We don’t have the permission, so we’ll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him..

Mittal said OneWeb’s ground network has been ready for three years, and its satellites have been hovering over India for five years, but the company is still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations.

His remarks come after Musk, the world’s richest man, accused powerful business interests of blocking Starlink’s entry into India. In a series of posts on social media platform X last week, Musk took aim at Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and questioning whether he wielded greater influence over India’s decisions than Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Musk has alleged that some business groups are seeking to preserve a “monopolistic chokehold” on Indian consumers. However, the Ministry of Communications has rejected the charge, describing suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application was unfair or discriminatory as “baseless and misconceived”.

The government said satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before they can begin commercial services.

Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said last week that three ventures — Musk’s Starlink, Reliance’s Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb — had secured satellite communications licences. Amazon’s Project Kuiper has expressed interest but must follow the established procedure, he said.

Scindia had said spectrum would be assigned once the government finalised a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfilled security requirements. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) were close to a decision on satellite spectrum pricing, he added.

The distinction between a licence and operational approval is central to the dispute: securing a licence does not automatically allow a company to begin commercial services. Spectrum assignment and the fulfilment of security conditions remain key steps.

The dispute comes at a consequential time for Reliance, which is preparing for the planned initial public offering of Jio Platforms, its digital services business. The proposed offering — the biggest so far in India — is expected to open on October 21 and values the company at about USD 106 billion.

Reliance is also developing its satellite ambitions, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites aimed at extending internet connectivity to 600,000 villages. That would put Jio in more direct competition with Starlink, which is seeking access to a vast market where satellite broadband could serve remote communities and locations poorly covered by terrestrial networks.

Ironically, Reliance and SpaceX last year signed an agreement to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio’s retail network.

Reliance’s Jio has already reported 524 million customers and extensive distribution capabilities, giving it a significant advantage in reaching consumers. Starlink, by contrast, would need to establish its customer base and operating model in India while meeting local requirements. PTI MBI ANZ MR

item.title: Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks
item.description: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Saul, Renee Maltezou
item.content:encoded: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway [USN:L1N45U0E0 TEXT:"have surged over the past 10 days"], with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources. "GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday. In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday. One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said. Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment. The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data. "MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law." GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment. "The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday. "The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage." IRAN TIGHTENS GRIP A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway. Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington. Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"two senior Iranian officials told Reuters."] While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk. The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.

item.title: Japan to invest up to $21 billion in two GlobalFoundries chip factories in New York
item.description: Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries , the company said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, David Shepardson, Makiko Yamazaki
item.content:encoded: Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries (GFS.O) , the company said on Wednesday. The initiative is part of a Trump administration deal struck last year for Japan to invest $550 billion in the US in return for the US lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25% to 15%. Shares of Malta, New York-based GlobalFoundries, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Co, rose more than 4% in afternoon trading. They have gained more than 39% this year. Construction of the first factory is scheduled to begin this year with chip production expected in 2029. GlobalFoundries executives said the partners will decide whether to build the second factory before the end of 2028. The first factory is expected to add annual US manufacturing capacity for about 900,000 300mm wafers when fully operational, ranking it among the larger US semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and create more than 1,000 factory jobs in New York. The US government previously held a 3% stake in GlobalFoundries. GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters that will rise to 7%. Japan will provide all of the investment capital under the deal. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the US government, which provided $1.63 billion in grants to the company, values the 7% stake in the company at more than $2 billion. "We are the first administration ever to turn grants into money for America," Trump said. Breen told Reuters initial customers for the New York factories include Japan's Renesas Electronics (6723.T) and iPhone maker Apple (AAPL.O) . On a conference call with investors, executives said the new deal will generate fees for the company for at least 20 years. This revenue is expected to be $50 million next year, when the company will earn fees for managing construction of the first factory. GlobalFoundries will shift $955 million previously awarded by the US government to accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium chip material and advanced packaging at its existing chip factories in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont. GlobalFoundries' Breen said that at least some of the capital investment by Japan will flow back to chip-manufacturing toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and other Japanese firms that along with US rivals dominate the supply chain. "Obviously, we have a strong interest in the Japanese equipment suppliers to be part of it," Breen said. "We will be very open-minded, but we'll definitely engage very much with the Japanese ecosystem because they have great technologies." Japan has so far announced two batches of projects worth over $100 billion combined under the overall investment scheme. Under the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flows from investments will be [USN:L1N42R099 TEXT:"split evenly"] between the two countries until a specific allocation is reached, after which 90% will go to the US. "We believe that working together with the US to expand semiconductor production capacity is highly significant for enhancing the economic security of both countries," Japanese Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa told reporters on Thursday. He rejected criticism that the investment initiative makes Japan subservient to the US, saying projects are subject to rigorous bilateral reviews to ensure they are financially viable, capable of repayment and beneficial to Japanese companies.

Yemen fighting overwhelms hospitals, cuts aid to 800,000 people, relief agencies say

Pieces of shattered glass are scattered across the floor of a hospital following an airstrike on a nearby building in Sanaa, Yemen on Oct 3, 2026. (File Photo: Reuters/Adel Al Khader)

GENEVA: Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Wednesday (Oct 14).

Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast are seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.

More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, according to the United Nations' International Organization for Migration.

A displaced Yemeni child sits under a tree as families gather to receive aid at the Al-Fallahine displacement camp in Dar Saad district, Aden, Yemen on Oct 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdulnasser Alseddik)

"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anesthesia, oxygen and medicines.

Yemen's health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, the ICRC warned.

The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz - Yemen's third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting - and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Programme said on Wednesday.

Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.

"This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most," said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement.

item.title: Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
item.description: The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan
item.content:encoded: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections . Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support. The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state. Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump. A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage [USN:L6N45U0XV TEXT:"to Democrats"] over his agenda. The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated [USN:L1N45R0LS TEXT:""toss-ups.""] One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held. Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races. Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat. Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base. 'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS' Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters. Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year. "I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said. Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported. "God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation. Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said. EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans. In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data. Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record. "Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union. Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear." The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law. The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices. NLRB 'DISMANTLING' When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly [USN:L2N3OO0LL TEXT:"fired"] two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted [USN:L1N3XM0FP TEXT:"for nearly a year."] Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies. "We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. [USN:L2N3S70NN TEXT:"Biden and Congress enacted programs"] to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors. Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said. OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets." A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns. Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote. Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners. "We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support. Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said. Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office. Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do." Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff."

item.title: China's Hesai launches spatial camera to boost AI-powered robotics adoption
item.description: Hesai Group , a leading Chinese autonomous driving technology firm, on Wednesday unveiled a three-dimensional mapping camera, targeting demand for physical spatial data needed to train the AI systems powering humanoid robots.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hesai Group (2525.HK) , a leading Chinese autonomous driving technology firm, on Wednesday unveiled a three-dimensional mapping camera, targeting demand for physical spatial data needed to train the AI systems powering humanoid robots. The company introduced "Kosmo," a device resembling a wine bottle, that combines lidar sensors and cameras to help developers collect real-world spatial data more efficiently. There is a significant gap in high-quality spatial data needed to train AI-powered robots to understand and interact with the real world and perform complex tasks beyond waving arms or dancing, Hesai co-founder and CEO David Li said at a launch event at the company's Shanghai factory. Li said robots remain limited in their ability to solve real productivity challenges. Most robots are still confined to low-impact functions like greeting guests, waving or dancing, he said. "What we aim to offer is essentially a platform for the underlying technologies required by the robotics industry, positioning Hesai as a tier 1 supplier comparable to Bosch in the automotive sector, or perhaps even beyond," Li said. He declined to provide revenue projections for Kosmo but said the firm has signed agreements with Chinese robotics firms to use the product. Hesai has also been developing robot actuators, which convert electricity into mechanical motion and account for more than half of a robot's material costs, Li said. Demand is growing for actuators that are lighter, smaller and more precise, allowing robots to become more safe and agile, he added. The actuators are already being used by Sharpa Robotics, a startup founded by Hesai's co-founders, in its flagship robotic hand, Sharpa Wave. A Sharpa Wave robot has been autonomously serving ice cream at a Dairy Queen outlet in Shanghai. Hesai said Kosmo's detailed mapping technology helped the robot achieve a task success rate of 99%. Sharpa Robotics, which recently raised more than 4.5 billion yuan ($672.4 million) in a funding round, operates independently of Hesai, but provides a testing ground for the company's robotics technologies. In automotive markets, Hesai has become the world's largest lidar supplier for autonomous vehicles over the past three years, driving the cost of the technology [USN:L3N3MX0MP TEXT:"below $200"] per unit. Its customers include Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) , Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) , General Motors (GM.N) and Ford Motor (F.N) . ($1 = 6.6923 Chinese yuan renminbi)
